label: paragraph_title
text: MR. D. K. BLAIR'S DEATH.

label: text
text: His War, Strike And Sport Work.

label: text
text: The death is announced in a brief cable which gives no details. of Mr. D. K. Blair, late Secretary of the Hongkong Chamber of Commerce. Death took place yesterday.

label: text
text: LATE MR. D.K. BLAIR.

label: text
text: A studio portrait of Mr. D. K. Blair, taken shortly before his departure for Home, after many years' residence in the Colony

label: text
text:
Whilst it will be a matter of grief to his many friends in Hong-
kong, to those who saw Mr. Blair at Home in the summer of last
year, the news will not come as a great shock.

label: text
text: Mr. Blair left Hongkong early in April, 1924. He had been in indifferent health and it was on medical advice that he left for Home.

label: text
text: He had served the Colony for many years and in different spheres and his judgment, discretion and long acquaintance with local conditions enabled him to fill with credit the responsible post he held when he left the Colony.

label: text
text: For his excellent work on behalf of the Colony, the late Mr. Blair was presented by the Government with a silver salver engraved with the Colony's emblem "as an indication of the appreciation of the Government of Hongkong of the services you have so willingly given on various occasions."

label: text
text: A sum of money was also voted to Mr. Blair by the Chamber of Commerce in order that he might purchase some memento as a mark of appreciation of his services.

label: text
text: When the Peak Hospital was handed over to the Government, Mr. Blair was appointed honorary secretary and treasurer. Mr. Blair reorganised the Hospital with such success that the Government was moved to express its warmest thanks "for" the very creditable manner" in which he "voluntarily carried out the arduous work." He also received a letter from the Colonial Treasurer expressing his sincere gratitude for all he had done, "in putting the Peak Hospital on a satisfactory basis both as regards efficiency and business matters."

label: text
text: Apart from his official work, Mr. Blair was best known as the Honorary Secretary of the St. Andrew's Society. The following tribute was paid to him by that Society on the occasion of his departure:—“As Secretary of the Society, you have placed the organisation at a high water mark of efficiency, and your personal interest and able management have been outstanding features in our Scottish celebrations.” Mr. Blair was a keen mason, being deputy master of Lodge Eastern Scotia, Number 923, of which he was also for many years a past master. His impending departure brought him a letter of sincere appreciation for his “many services and unequalled generosity;” and the lodge also presented him with suitably inscribed emblems of the craft as a souvenir.

label: text
text: During his residence in Hongkong, Mr. Blair took the keenest interest in yachting and together with Mr. Frank Smyth his name will long be remembered as prominently associated with the progress of the Royal Hongkong Yacht Club. For many years Mr. Blair was Sailing Secretary and he did splendid work in connection with the Club's annual regattas. It was in recognition of his hard work as an official of that Club that he was made Vice-Commodore and later Commodore, which position he held at the time of his departure from the Colony.

label: text
text: Before he left, Mr. Blair was the recipient of a handsome solid silver cigar and cigarette box, the gift of prominent members of the Yacht Club whose signatures were inscribed on it.

label: text
text: Mr. Blair was a Justice of the Peace for Hongkong

label: text
text: Mr. Blair was a native of Irvine, Ayrshire. He first came to the East in 1889 and was originally in the service of the Eastern Extension Telegraph Company serving Shanghai and North China as well as Hongkong. During the Boxer rebellion he was in the North and helped to maintain telegraph services at Tientsin and Taku forts during those hazardous times.

label: text
text: The late Mr. Blair came to Hongkong as Assistant Secretary of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce. Having acted as Secretary on numerous occasions, he was appointed Secretary in 1921.

label: text
text: During the Seamen's Strike, tribute was paid by the Government to Mr. Blair's excellent work "which had been of the greatest assistance" in conducting to the smooth running of the services.

label: text
text: Another branch of his earlier activities was that in connection with the raising of a Signalling Section of the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps during the War when he trained many residents in the art of telegraphic signalling. He remained with his section until it was desbanded.

label: text
text:
Much sympathy will be felt with the late Mr. Blair's family.

label: text
text: Although, owing to certain factors, the directors of the Hongkong, Canton, and Macao Steamboat Co., Ltd, announce no dividend for the year, a sound position as regards the balance sheet and working generally was disclosed at the annual meeting this morning.

label: text
text: The Chairman, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, in the course of his statement, said that he had reason to believe that the Company would receive financial support from the Government in meeting the loss involved in keeping up communication between Hongkong and Shameen.

label: text
text: The following were present:—The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak (Chairman), the Hon. Mr. A. O. Lang, Messrs. W. E. Clarke, T. G. Weall, J. M. Alves, H. Staples Smith, and R. M. Austin (Directors), Mr. John Arnold (Secretary), also the following shareholders:—Messrs. S. H. Michael, L. S. Greenhill, Cheng Ching-po, S. Danenberg, J. Owen Hughes, Paul Lauder, G. E. Townes, and Geo. S. Zimmern.

label: paragraph_title
text: Chairman's Speech

label: text
text: The Chairman said: — The directors' report and auditors' statements having been in your hands for some days, I propose with your consent to follow the usual custom of taking them as read.

label: text
text: you will, I am sure, realise that it is difficult "and indeed would be unwise for me to dwell at length on the incidents of the past seven months which are common knowledge to you all." Under all the circumstances, the balance sheet may be considered satisfactory. For the first six months of the year, our trading results compared very favourably with the average figures of preceding years and given normal times we feel certain we could have set before you a good balance sheet. The year has been marked by the strike in June and the subsequent boycott of British shipping in South China. Our Macao service was suspended from June 18 to July 27 when one boat was put on the run. Less than a month later, August 22, the full service to Macao was resumed. In September, at the request of the authorities, and in the consultation with the Government, the "Honam" re-opened the Canton sailing and we have maintained our Cantonsailings continuously ever since. It was obvious that the boats could not earn a profit but it was felt by your directors that it was in the interests of all to maintain communication with Shameen and Canton and our flag upon the river. I have reason to believe that we shall receive financial support from the Government in meeting the loss which has been involved in giving vital and essential service, which is not likely to be forgotten by our loyal supporters, Chinese as well as foreign, when times are once more normal and our fleet is in full operation. It is fitting here that I should record the high appreciation of your directors of the services of the floating staff under especially the trying conditions which have prevailed. label: text
text: Addressing the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps on the 8th inst. His Excellency the Governor said: "H.E. the G.O.C. considers, and I am sure you will all agree, that the present period of your annual training is too short and I propose to see whether suitable arrangements cannot forthwith be made for prolonging it. I am also at the suggestion of H.M.'s Government inquiring whether it would not be possible to form in Hongkong a corps of Naval Volunteers, in addition to the units which already exist. Both these projects will soon come up for public discussion and I trust that you and the whole community will give full support to any well-considered schemes which the military and naval authorities devise for enlisting additional help from civilians in the defence of this Colony."

label: text

label: text
text: He says that although there has been an absence up to the present of any occasion for spectacular exercise, this responsibility in the general conduct of the world's affairs no doubt prevented the Western people's recognition of such consistent with its importance.

label: text

The voice of Japan nevertheless was ever present in the inner Council Chambers of the world.
Earon Matsuł declares that Japan does not sympathise with the suggestion of a combination of Oriental peoples against Europe, though she is not unmindful of the ties binding her to her fellow-Asiatics. Her first and constant endeavours are to keep on good terms with her immediate neighbours.

label: text

The idea will be also, to arrange the duties similarly to those in connection with the Volunteers, in order that business may be interfered with as little as possible. Patrol work and (in case of war) mine sweeping or mine-laying would be among the matters which such a corps would be able to attend to. In cases of emergency such as arose a short time back, the naval reserve would be invaluable in the maintenance of communication between the island and the mainland and other special work. The organisation would be under naval discipline.
That the organisation of such a Reserve is practicable has been proved elsewhere. In Singapore, a unit consisting of over 50 men was formed almost immediately the scheme was announced and numbers are growing. In Ceylon, a similar scheme is in working operation. Hongkong, as one of the most important outposts of the Empire, is dependent for its prosperity on the maintenance of its shipping connections. The formation of a Reserve for its protection would be a very practical contribution to the problem of Imperial Defence. It may safely be said that once the appeal is launched there will be no lack of volunteers.
